name: Carlos Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a lettings negotiator at Harlow & Pike, the branch on Station Road. Most mornings I'm out with the keys by half nine, showing flats to people who've seen them on the portals, then back to chase references and deposits. I like the viewings, honestly, meeting a nurse who needs to be near the hospital and actually finding her something. What wears me out is the system, the screens, Denise (my manager) asking why my notes aren't on the CRM when I've written them in my diary.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Paper, yeah, a blue one from the corner shop. I've been here eighteen months, before that I was waiting tables, and I still don't trust the software to remember things the way I do. Priya (the senior negotiator) laughs at me, but she also asks me which tenant had the dog, because I wrote it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, so the boring one. I can picture that, because that's sort of what it's been like so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. Everyone at the branch was saying the chatbot would do half our job, and it ended up writing listings nobody reads. I'd say people still want a person to show them round and to ring when the boiler breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my problem was never AI, it's rent and targets. I pay 720 a month for a room in a three-bed share, and my commission swings from 300 to almost nothing depending on the month. Denise puts the board up every Monday with everyone's lets, and my name's usually near the bottom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, basically. I'd keep doing the viewings and keep my diary, and maybe finally learn the CRM properly because Denise isn't going to stop asking. I'd try to put 100 a month away so my cushion goes from about three months to four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly, but not relaxed. The ground under me is the same ground, and it was already a bit wobbly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your name's near the bottom of the board. What happens if it stays there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I get the talk, I suppose. Marcus (a junior on the sales side) got it last spring, they gave him three months to turn it around and he did, just. Nobody at my agency gets sacked by a robot, they get sacked by the Monday board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the pressure, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The landlords with twenty flats, and the portals charging the agency more every year, so the agency squeezes us. I'm not saying the bosses are evil, Denise has her own targets. But the whole thing's set up so the people at the bottom carry the risk.

say: I'd say the **AI hype** fizzled and people still want a **real person** at viewings.
I'd tell friends my job is **fine**, it's renting that's hard.
think: My real worry is the **Monday board**, where my lets sit near the bottom.
Paying **720 a month** for a room on swinging **commission** leaves little room for error.
do: Keep doing **viewings** and keep the paper diary going.
Learn the **CRM** properly so Denise stops chasing me about notes.
Save **100 a month** to stretch the cushion from three months to four.
feel: **Relieved** that nothing big changes, but still **wobbly** about money.
S0.quote: Nobody at my agency gets sacked by a robot, they get sacked by the Monday board.
fieldNote: Carlos frames his insecurity as **targets and rent**, not technology; AI barely registers in this world.
He keeps a **paper diary** and resists the CRM, a small sign of how he meets new tools.
Blames **big landlords and portals** for squeezing juniors, while defending his manager personally.

steps.text: Keep showing flats every morning and logging tenants in the paper diary
Put 100 a month into savings to reach four months' cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's closer to home. The booking and answering bit is half my afternoons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say it's a tool and tools don't show flats. I'd post something about how renters deserve a human when the landlord won't fix the damp, not a chatbot. I'd probably share stuff from the renters' groups about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the part of my job that's chasing references, booking viewings and answering the same five questions on email is the part they'd hand over first. That's maybe half my day. If Harlow & Pike can do it with three negotiators instead of five, the two who go are the two at the bottom of the board, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join a union, even though nobody at the branch is in one, probably the general workers' one my cousin's in. I'd stop spending on takeaways and try to get to five months saved. And I'd ask Priya to show me whatever new system they bring in, slowly, because I'd rather learn it from her than from a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Like I'm being lined up for something and I can't see who's holding the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the system from Priya. Before, you said you never use AI tools. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I guess. I don't want to use it, but if keeping my job means pressing the buttons, I'll press them. I'm not going to lose my job over a blue paper diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government or anyone else to do in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rules, basically. If an agency cuts staff because the software does the booking, tenants should still have a named person they can ring. And some help to retrain that isn't a website telling you to learn coding.

say: I'd say renters deserve a **human contact**, not a chatbot, when the damp isn't fixed.
I'd share posts from **renters' groups** pushing back on agencies replacing staff.
think: Booking, references and email replies are about **half my day**, the first part to go.
If the branch drops to three negotiators, the **bottom of the board** goes, meaning me.
do: Join the **general union** my cousin belongs to, even with no members at work.
Cut takeaways and push savings towards **five months**.
Ask Priya to teach me the **new system** slowly, in person.
feel: **Tight-chested**, like being on a **list** I can't see.
S1.quote: I'm not going to lose my job over a blue paper diary.
fieldNote: Carlos sees clearly that the **desk half** of lettings is the exposed half.
His dislike of AI gives way to **grudging use** once his job depends on it.
He reaches for **unions and rules** before personal reinvention.

steps.text: Join the general workers' union his cousin belongs to
Stop buying takeaways and build savings to five months
Have Priya teach him the agency's new booking software in person

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before my contract's even up for its next review, basically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd be angry, I think. I'd say this was done to people, not for them, and that the companies making money from it should pay for the people it pushes out. I'd go to whatever protest the union called.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished in lettings within a year of it arriving. The listings, the referencing, the valuations, the emails, that's all thinking work and it'd go in 2028. The viewings would last until the robots come around 2031, but I don't think Harlow & Pike pays someone just to open doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd stop all the extras and get every spare pound into savings, so maybe six months by the time it lands. If the branch starts cutting, I'd move back into my mum's spare room across town to stop paying 720 rent. I'd sign every petition and go on every march for a support payment for people pushed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. Scared and a bit embarrassed, because at 27 I thought I'd be moving forward, not back into my old bedroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum when you asked to move back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's not forever, which I wouldn't know. She'd say yes before I finished the sentence, that's the kind of person she is. Moving back into my mum's spare room at 27 isn't a plan, it's a parachute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about 3 years after the thinking AI. Does that gap help you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, for doing viewings or maybe inventory check-ins, the walking-round part. But that's three years of being the person who holds the keys while a computer does the actual job. I'd use those years to find something hands-on that people still want a human for, maybe care work, I just don't know what yet.

say: I'd say AGI was **done to people**, and the companies profiting should **pay** for it.
I'd show up at any **protest** the union organised.
think: The thinking side of lettings goes in **2028**, and I'd likely be out **within a year**.
Viewings last until robots arrive around **2031**, but nobody pays just to **open doors**.
do: Put every spare pound into savings, aiming for **six months** before it lands.
Move back into **my mum's** spare room if the branch starts cutting.
Sign petitions and march for a **support payment** for displaced workers.
feel: **Scared** about losing the job and **embarrassed** about moving backwards at 27.
S2.quote: Moving back into my mum's spare room at 27 isn't a plan, it's a parachute.
fieldNote: Carlos expects to **lose his job** soon after 2028 and says so plainly.
His safety net is **family**, specifically his mum's spare room, which he calls a parachute.
He has **no clear next job**, only a vague pull towards hands-on care work.

steps.text: Cancel extras and save every spare pound towards six months
Move into his mum's spare room if Harlow & Pike cuts staff
Join union marches and petitions for a support payment
Look for hands-on work like care jobs during the robot gap

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's 2031 for the desk side, and the robots by 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, that we need rules before it lands, not after. But I'd probably say it louder, because five years is enough time for a government to actually do something if people push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years means I'm 32 when it hits. I'd have maybe got a bit better at the job by then, but not senior enough to matter. The part that worries me is I'm the kind of person who waits, and five years is exactly the length of time I'd waste.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write to my local councillor and vote for whoever promises retraining money with actual teachers in it. I'd look at the housing association, they have tenancy officer jobs, and that's lettings but with tenants' rights, which is more me. And I'd keep saving, maybe 150 a month, because the gap between jobs is what kills you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less like I'm falling. More like I'm watching a slow wave come in and I'm not sure I'll move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the housing association, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's public, sort of, and slower to change. And I'd be on the tenants' side for once instead of the landlord's. A housing association job is still a desk job, I know that, it just buys me a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might not move in time. What would make you actually do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone at work going first. If Priya left or got cut, I'd panic and apply that week. That's not a great way to run your life, I know.

say: I'd push for **rules before** AGI lands, not after.
I'd say five years is **long enough** for government to act if people push.
think: I'd be **32** when it hits, still not senior enough to be safe.
I'm a **waiter-for-signs**, and five years is exactly the time I'd waste.
do: Write to the **local councillor** and vote for real retraining money.
Apply for **tenancy officer** jobs at the housing association.
Raise saving to **150 a month** to cover a gap between jobs.
feel: **Worried**, like watching a **slow wave** come in and not moving.
S3.quote: A housing association job is still a desk job, I know that, it just buys me a few more years.
fieldNote: Carlos knows his own habit of **waiting** and names it as his main risk.
The **housing association** appeals for both values and slower change, though he admits it's still desk work.
He would only act when a **colleague goes first**.

steps.text: Write to the local councillor about funded retraining with real teachers
Apply for tenancy officer jobs at the housing association
Raise monthly saving to 150 to cover a gap between jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036 for the desk work, 2039 for the robots. I'd be 37.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse for the government not to have a plan. I'd be the one in the group chat saying don't let them tell us it's our fault for not retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me relax, and that's the danger. I'd probably keep doing lettings for five or six years, keep my diary, and only look up when it's close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, honestly, not much. I'd keep showing flats and keep saving. Maybe around year five I'd do a proper course, something like a gas safety or property maintenance certificate, because the robots come three years after and that's the side I'd want to be on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Not calm, because I know it's coming, but there's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait five years before a course. What would you say to yourself at 32 if that was too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say you knew. That's the thing, I'd know I knew. Ten years feels like forever when you're 27, and I've watched my dad say that about his pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad's pension have to do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He always said he'd sort it later, and later came. He's 61 now and still driving a delivery van. I don't want to be the version of him that's still holding keys at 50 when nobody needs keys.

say: I'd say a **decade** leaves the government **no excuse** for having no plan.
I'd push back on any line that it's **our fault** for not retraining.
think: Ten years makes me **relax**, and that's exactly the **danger** for me.
I'd likely stay in lettings **five or six years** before looking up.
do: Keep showing flats and **saving** steadily this year.
Take a **property maintenance** or gas safety course around year five.
feel: **Calmer**, with **room to breathe**, though I know it's still coming.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like forever when you're 27, and I've watched my dad say that about his pension.
fieldNote: Carlos sees his own **procrastination** clearly, linking it to his father's **late pension** planning.
The robot gap pulls him towards **hands-on maintenance** skills, but only later.
He still expects to **lose lettings work** eventually, so the decade eases rather than removes worry.

steps.text: Keep showing flats at the Station Road branch and saving monthly
Wait until about year five before choosing a course
Take a property maintenance or gas safety course around 2031

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easy. Two years isn't enough for someone like me, who takes a year to learn a new screen. What would help is a support payment while you retrain, and real people teaching the courses, not apps. I can learn anything if someone stands next to me and shows me, I just can't learn it from a screen telling me I'm behind.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about tenants. Everyone talks about agents losing jobs, but if nobody's left to ring when the boiler breaks, it's the renters who get hurt. I'd want someone to think about them too.

headlineQuote: I can learn anything if someone stands next to me and shows me, I just can't learn it from a screen telling me I'm behind.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old** lettings negotiator at Harlow & Pike, eighteen months in, after years waiting tables.
He keeps a **paper diary**, avoids the CRM and never uses AI tools.
His pressures are **rent and targets**: a 720 room and a Monday board where he ranks low.
As AGI speeds up he moves from **saving** and union membership to falling back on **his mum**.
He knows he tends to **wait**, and fears wasting whatever warning time he gets.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short for someone who learns **slowly**.
whatWouldHelp: A **support payment** while retraining, and courses taught by **real people** in person.
